title: The good point (Likutey Moharan 282)
hookLine: Rebbe Nachman: find the good point in another person, and in yourself, and it lifts them
tomorrow: an hour a day talking to God, in your own words. really?

lines: ONE BAD POST, AND THAT'S WHO THEY ARE.
cards: A screenshot of someone's worst moment can travel fast. One bad post, and that's who they are now. There's a verse in the Psalms that seems to agree.
Psalm thirty-seven: a little while longer, and the wicked one is gone; you'll look closely at his place, and he isn't there. It reads like a promise that bad people simply vanish.
Rebbe Nachman of Breslov read the same verse and heard hope, and something more: instructions. So what did he spot that the rest of us read straight past?

teach.b: Two small Hebrew words near the start: od me'at, a little more, a little while. Rebbe Nachman reads them as: look for a little more.
In the person who seems wholly wicked, find a little bit of good, a nekudah tovah, a good point. Something, somewhere, he did right.

When you judge him by that point, he teaches in Likutey Moharan, teaching 282, you really do lift him toward the side of merit. Then the end of the verse comes true in a new way. You look at his place, and he isn't there.

teach.h: HE'S NO LONGER WHERE HE STOOD.
teach.b: Not because he vanished, but because he's no longer standing where he was. That's the puzzle solved. The verse isn't about erasing a person.
It's about finding the point that moves them. Then he turns it around, and this is the part people pass on. Do the same for yourself.
When you look inside and see mostly failure, don't stop there.
Search for one good point that's really yours, and then another.
He ties it to a second verse, where the psalmist sings to God while he still has his being, and hears it as: with the little good still in me.
Those good points, gathered one by one, he says, are like notes, and a melody is made from them. A teaching that starts with the worst person in the room ends as a song about you.

how: Breslov Hasidim study Rebbe Nachman's teaching on the good point, known by its opening word Azamra, 'I will sing', and it is often taught as a way to judge others, and oneself, favorably.

o: the bit of real good you look for in a person, and in yourself
the moment in a trial when the judge decides who is right
the main argument of a sermon, said once more at the very end

games.q: how the puzzle is solved — tap the pairs.
p: a little more, a little while
a good point in a person
no longer standing where he was

s: Rebbe Nachman reads Psalm 37 as a promise that the wicked simply vanish
he reads 'a little more' as: find a little good, and the person is no longer where he stood.
he says to search for good points in yourself, not only in others
one good point, then another, gathered like notes into a melody.
finding someone's good point means pretending they did nothing wrong
the verse calls him wicked; you judge him by the good point anyway, and that lifts him.

games.q: your little brother broke your headphones and then lied about it. your parents ask what you think should happen. what would Rebbe Nachman's good point add?
o: name the lie, and also one real good thing you know is in him.
the lie is what matters now, so keep the focus there and only there.
let it go without a word, so nobody's mood gets worse tonight.
games.why: Likutey Moharan 282 doesn't pretend the wrong away. it says judging a person by their good point lifts them toward merit.

practice: Get a pen and a scrap of paper. Write the first name of someone you've written off lately, and next to it one good point that's really there, small is fine.
Underneath, write one good point of your own, and let your eyes rest on both lines for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The good point: Rebbe Nachman's nekudah tovah. The bit of real good in a person, which, when you judge by it, lifts them, and you.

orig.note: Hebrew: a good point; Rebbe Nachman's phrase for the bit of good to look for in another person and in yourself.

carryVoice: Here's the line: find the good point, in them first and then, harder, in you. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Likutey Moharan I:282 (Azamra: find the good point in another, judge favorably, and he is lifted; then find good points in yourself; the good points make a melody)
